tldr: By discarding heavy video generation backbones and training a small policy from scratch directly in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA encoder, this world-action model achieves drastic reductions in compute, much faster inference, and state-of-the-art manipulation performance.
hero_caption: Four manipulation tasks evaluated on a real Franka Emika (Franka Panda) robot. From left to right: Cube Placement, Fruit Picking (opening a steamer lid to retrieve a plum), the contact-rich Push-T task, and a long-horizon Table Setting task arranging two plates and cutlery.
overview:
In recent robot manipulation, adopting pretrained video generators or large vision-language models (VLMs) as policy backbones (world-action models or VLAs) has become the dominant approach. However, these models inherit massive transformers originally designed for "generation" tasks like pixel reconstruction. This results in heavy inference costs and raises the question of whether generation-oriented architectures are truly optimal for control.

To address this, the authors hypothesized that control does not require precise pixel reconstruction, but rather rich visual representations well-suited for downstream tasks. They propose Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), which adopts the latent space of self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 and trains a compact transformer from scratch to jointly predict future features and actions. By following Fast-WAM's design—learning future predictions during training to enrich representations, while completely bypassing future prediction at inference to output only actions—unnecessary computation is eliminated.

When evaluated on simulation benchmarks like RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Plus, as well as four real Franka tasks, La-JEPA achieved SOTA performance among policies without embodied pretraining. It runs up to 5x faster than the strong Fast-WAM baseline and matches the success rate of large, pretrained models on real robot hardware.
contributions: Proposed Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, discarding heavy video generation backbones.

Combined latent future feature prediction at training time with an action-only execution pathway at inference, achieving up to 5x faster inference with roughly one-fourth the deployed parameter count of competing models.
Achieved state-of-the-art generalization on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Plus among policies without embodied pretraining, and matched the success rate of large VLAs on real-robot tasks.

Provided detailed design ablations covering video VAE latents vs. JEPA feature spaces, camera dropout, and other choices, offering clear guidelines to boost control performance and out-of-distribution robustness.
Discovered and corrected an instruction-corruption bug (text leakage) in the official LIBERO-Plus evaluation benchmark, re-evaluating strong open baselines in a fair environment.

sections.heading: Freeing Robot Policies from the Heavy Baggage of Generative Models
sections.summary: Existing world-action models and VLAs inherit massive backbones designed for video or language generation, but pixel-level reconstruction capability is superfluous for control. This paper introduces La-JEPA, a compact world-action model trained from scratch on V-JEPA representation space designed specifically for control.
sections.details:
In modern robot learning, world-action models (WAMs) that adapt video generation transformers and vision-language-action (VLA) policies built on vision-language models have gained massive traction. While they leverage rich visual and temporal knowledge acquired via large-scale pretraining, they also inherit huge architectures and tokenization structures with hundreds of millions to billions of parameters designed for video synthesis and text generation.

In particular, many WAMs operate on the latent space of video Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). Because VAEs spend a large portion of their capacity preserving pixel-level fidelity, they tend to retain redundant information irrelevant to robot control. In contrast, representations learned by Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)—which predict embeddings of masked inputs—are optimized for high-level recognition tasks like video understanding and segmentation, making them far better suited for embodied robot control.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA). It learns future feature prediction and action generation directly inside the dense feature space provided by a pretrained, frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Because the policy transformer itself is built from scratch with a small footprint, its capacity and architecture can be chosen purely for control without generative constraints.

As a result, La-JEPA deploys with roughly four times fewer parameters than strong competing baselines, runs up to 5x faster than Fast-WAM, and achieves top-tier success rates in both simulation and real-robot evaluations.

sections.heading: VLAs, World Models, and JEPAs: Where Compact Policies Stand
sections.summary: Conventional VLAs and video WAMs rely heavily on giant pretrained backbones, while compact policies have historically lagged in performance. By uniting JEPA's superior representations with Fast-WAM's decoupled training and inference, La-JEPA establishes a unique position: lightweight yet capable of outperforming massive models.
sections.details:
Prior work surrounding this research can be categorized into four primary groups:

### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Policies
These policies add action token prediction heads or flow-matching action experts onto pretrained VLMs. While they show strong generalization, they require running billions of backbone parameters at inference time, making computation extremely heavy.

### World-Action Models (WAMs)
These approaches harness representations from image and video generation models for action prediction. Because generating future video frames at inference leads to massive latency, recent methods like Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM have emerged to predict future frames only during training and output solely actions at test time. Even so, they still inherit the bulky structures of underlying video generators.

### Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)
Rather than reconstructing pixels, this framework predicts within an abstract feature space. V-JEPA 2.1 provides dense, temporal representations ideal for robotics. Previous works such as JEPA-WAM and LeapBot-WA also explored V-JEPA, but they continued to repurpose existing VLMs or video generators for their predictors.

### Compact Policies
Lightweight policies trained from scratch, such as Diffusion Policy and ACT, have generally trailed behind large WAMs and VLAs in performance. La-JEPA belongs to this compact category, yet it outperforms giant models by combining high-quality JEPA representations with an auxiliary future prediction task during training.

sections.heading: Inside La-JEPA: A Lightweight World-Action Model in V-JEPA Space
sections.summary: La-JEPA takes V-JEPA 2.1 visual features, FLAN-T5 language instructions, and proprioception as input, utilizing two independent, compact diffusion transformers: World DiT and Action DiT. During training, both are trained via joint flow matching; at inference, observation features are cached to quickly integrate actions alone.
sections.details:
La-JEPA's overall architecture and inference pipeline are streamlined specifically for control.

### 3.1 Architecture
- Visual Representations: Uses a pretrained and frozen V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L encoder. Observation features $z_{\mathrm{ctx}}$ are extracted from the latest frames, while target features $z_{\mathrm{fut}}$ cover up to 32 frames into the future. There is no separate RGB image processing path, and no pixel reconstruction is performed.
- Language and Proprioception: Instructions are embedded using a frozen FLAN-T5-large encoder, while proprioceptive state $s_t$ (e.g., robot joint states) is linearly projected to form conditioning tokens $z_{\mathrm{cond}}$.
- World and Action DiTs: The model consists of two Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) initialized from scratch: the World DiT, which processes context and future tokens, and the Action DiT, which handles continuous action chunks. Attention masks strictly control information flow: action tokens can attend to context tokens, but cannot see future tokens. This ensures that the auxiliary future prediction loss provides a strong gradient signal to train context representations through shared parameters.

### 3.2 Training and Inference
- Joint Flow Matching: During training, noise timesteps $\tau_f$ for future features and $\tau_a$ for actions are sampled independently to predict velocity fields $\hat{v}_f$ and $\hat{v}_a$. The total loss is the sum of mean squared errors for both.
- Action Inference: At test time, future prediction tokens are discarded entirely. By fixing the context timestep conditioning to $\tau_{\mathrm{ctx}}=0$, context tokens attend only to themselves. Consequently, the Key and Value states at each layer can be computed once and cached. The Action DiT then simply integrates over noise via Euler steps (typically 10 steps, down to 3) to generate action chunks, enabling an ultra-low-latency control loop.

sections.heading: Why Does It Work? Ablations on Feature Space, Temporal Encoding, and Robustness
sections.summary: The authors systematically ablated each design choice. Future feature prediction, the overwhelming superiority of V-JEPA over video VAE latents, and robustness techniques like camera and proprioception dropout drastically boost success rates, especially in out-of-distribution settings.
sections.details:
Using the baseline model (Small size, 0.1B trainable parameters), the impact of key design choices was thoroughly investigated.

### 4.1 Prediction Targets and Feature Spaces
- Auxiliary Future Prediction: Predicting future features jointly provided significant gains over learning actions alone: +7.0 points in RoboTwin clean environments, +3.7 points in randomized environments, and an average of +2.1 points on LIBERO-Plus.
- Feature Space Selection (V-JEPA vs. Wan2.2 VAE): Comparing the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 space against the latent space of the Wan2.2 video VAE (used in Fast-WAM), the difference was stark: V-JEPA outperformed Wan2.2 by +15.9 points in clean settings and +16.0 points in randomized settings. Under randomized perturbations, the Wan2.2 model's success rate collapsed to 1.0%, proving that high-level JEPA representations are indispensable for control.
- Temporal Encoding: Compared to a static frame-by-frame approach, adopting Tube encoding (2-frame clips) and Tube-motion encoding (jointly encoding 16 future frames) provided an improvement of +3.4 points in clean and +3.7 points in randomized conditions.
- Token Reduction: For spatial compression, simple mean pooling was sufficient on LIBERO, whereas patch grouping—which concatenates features—proved beneficial in RoboTwin's randomized environments where fine geometric details matter.

### 4.2 Robustness and Encoder Adaptation
- Camera and Proprioception Dropout: Randomly dropping out camera inputs (e.g., wrist camera) during training reduced over-reliance on specific viewpoints, yielding a massive boost of +7.1 points in RoboTwin randomized and +10.2 points on LIBERO-Plus. Dropping proprioception with a probability of 0.1 also yielded an approximate 4-point improvement.
- Image Augmentations and Encoder LoRA: Combining visual augmentations on context images with LoRA adaptation of the visual encoder delivered large gains: +7.2 points on LIBERO-Plus and +16.0 points on RoboTwin randomized. To conserve compute, future targets were precomputed once using the frozen encoder on unaugmented images.

sections.heading: Empirical Proof: SOTA Performance and Speed in Sim and Real Robots
sections.summary: La-JEPA achieves the highest benchmark scores among non-embodied-pretrained policies. It runs up to 5x faster than Fast-WAM, and on four real Franka tasks, it approaches the success rate of the large-scale pretrained model π0.5 while demonstrating swifter execution.
sections.details:
The authors benchmarked the final recipe across three model sizes (S: 0.10B, B: 0.34B, L: 1.14B).

### 5.1 Benchmark Performance and Generalization
On RoboTwin 2.0 (both clean and randomized settings), all three La-JEPA sizes completely surpassed existing non-embodied-pretrained baselines. On LIBERO-Plus, performance scaled consistently with model size, and under the corrected instruction protocol, La-JEPA L achieved the top score, beating NowWAM by 1.8 points. Furthermore, even compared to models with large-scale embodied pretraining (such as OLA-Sem and GigaBrain), La-JEPA B performed competitively near the top tier.

### 5.2 LIBERO-Plus Instruction Leakage Bug
A key secondary contribution of this study is identifying that the official LIBERO-Plus evaluation script corrupted instructions for 8,493 out of 10,030 variants by erroneously appending perturbation parameters to the text strings. Re-evaluating baselines with this corruption removed revealed that video-based WAMs (like Fast-WAM) had been severely underestimated by up to 19.3 points due to language sensitivity, establishing a fair evaluation setting.

### 5.3 Head-to-Head Against Latent World Models
Against competing models that also leverage V-JEPA (such as LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM), La-JEPA held a substantial lead. On the 20 RoboTwin tasks evaluated by JEPA-WAM, La-JEPA outperformed it by over 15 points in clean and over 9 points in randomized conditions.

### 5.4 Computational Cost and Inference Latency
La-JEPA runs effortlessly on a single consumer GPU. With compilation optimizations, a 10-denoising-step policy call takes just 19ms for the S size and 26ms for B, running 2x to 5x faster than Fast-WAM (92ms) and Faster-WAM (54ms). Reducing denoising to 3 steps only dropped success by ~1 point, offering a notable advantage for real-time control.

### 5.5 Real-Robot Experiments
Using a Franka Panda arm, La-JEPA B trained from scratch on 100 demonstrations per task was evaluated on hardware across four tasks: Cube Placement, Fruit Picking (from a steamer), contact-heavy Push-T, and multi-step Table Setting (arranging two plates and cutlery). La-JEPA achieved the highest average success rate among models without embodied pretraining, and even surpassed the pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$ model on the contact-intensive Push-T task. It also completed successful trials faster and with greater agility than baseline methods.

captions.F5: Four real-robot tasks on a Franka Panda (from left: Cube Placement, Fruit Picking, Push-T, and Table Setting). La-JEPA achieved the highest success rate on the contact-heavy Push-T task and demonstrated stable control in the multi-step Table Setting task.

sections.heading: Looking Ahead: Scaling Challenges and Pretraining Opportunities
sections.summary: Because this study focused on training from scratch using target demonstrations, understanding scaling properties when combined with large-scale robot pretraining remains an open challenge. Exhaustive hyperparameter tuning and cross-embodiment generalization also require further study.
sections.details:
While La-JEPA demonstrated outstanding performance, the authors note several limitations and future avenues:

- Scope of Recipe Optimization: The paper aimed to establish the potential of compact designs rather than conducting exhaustive sweeps over learning rates, weight decays, LoRA placements, or the capacity balance between World and Action DiTs. On RoboTwin, performance did not scale strictly monotonically with model size, potentially pointing to Action DiT overfitting or demonstration data constraints, which warrant further isolation.
- Integration with Large-Scale Embodied Pretraining: La-JEPA was trained purely on demonstration data from target tasks. How these representations and policy architectures scale when pretrained on broad robotic datasets remains unknown. Extending the framework to multi-task pretraining across diverse embodiments and environments is the most promising path to close the remaining gap with top-tier pretrained models in randomized settings.

sections.heading: Takeaway: A Control-Centric Representation Space Unlocks Efficient Policies
sections.summary: La-JEPA proves that robot policies do not need to inherit heavy generative backbones. By utilizing JEPA feature spaces designed for downstream tasks, policies achieve both state-of-the-art control performance and rapid inference, providing an important stepping stone for robot foundation models.
sections.details:
To the question "Must robot policies inherit the architectures of giant image and video generators?", this paper offers a resounding "No."

By training a compact, control-tailored transformer from scratch within the refined latent space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, La-JEPA surpasses larger models across benchmark evaluations and maintains exceptional robustness against disturbances. Furthermore, by skipping redundant future predictions during inference, it delivers the ultra-low latency demanded by real-time hardware control.

By shedding the burden of pixel reconstruction and refocusing on what representations control actually needs, this work offers crucial architectural insights for the future of robot foundation models.

takeaways: Pretrained V-JEPA feature representations are vastly superior to pixel-reconstructing video VAE latents for robot control, especially in maintaining robustness against environment variations.

Adding an auxiliary future feature prediction task during training significantly enriches observation representations and improves policy success, even when future prediction is completely skipped at inference.
Caching context Key/Value tokens at inference while integrating only the small Action DiT yields 2x to 5x faster inference speeds compared to conventional video WAMs.
Combining camera viewpoint and proprioception dropout with encoder LoRA adaptation dramatically enhances out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.
limitations: Performance did not scale monotonically with model size on RoboTwin, leaving open questions on capacity balancing and data saturation to prevent Action DiT overfitting.

The model does not employ large-scale multi-task robot pretraining (embodied pretraining), showing some remaining performance gaps against massive pretrained models in heavily randomized environments.
Real-robot validation was confined to four tabletop manipulation tasks on a single Franka arm; testing generalization across broader, more dynamic manipulation setups remains for future work.
